# Data Visualization for Halloween 

Ensure that you have the following two lines of code at the top of `lab-05.Rmd` to make the commands available to you.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Install that package first 
# install.packages("fivethirtyeight")
library(fivethirtyeight)
```


```{r}
candy_df <- candy_rankings
glimpse(candy_df)
```


## Exercise 1

How many observations and variables are in this dataset?
Did you identify the type of variables, remember that this detail is crucial to create which kind of data visualization in general. 

_There are 85-1=84 observations and 13 variables. There is 1 character variable, 3 double variables and 9 logical variables._

# Data viz - One variable at a time

Just to use the logical variables as categories, run the following code chunk first!

```{r}
candy_df <- candy_df %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), as_factor))
```

## Exercise 2

Complete the following code to get the data viz to represent "how many candies contain caramel via bar plot". Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_rankings, aes(x = caramel)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = 'Number of candies containing caramel',
    x = 'Contains caramel',
    y = 'Count'
    )

ggplot(candy_rankings, aes(x = chocolate)) +
  geom_bar() + 
  labs(
    title = 'Number of candies containing chocolate',
    x = 'Contains chocolate',
    y = 'Count'
  )
```

## Exercise 3

Now look at a numerical variable, such as `winpercent`. Create an histogram for this variable using ggplot2 functions below. Include informative x and y labels and a title, as a good practice.

```{r}
candy_rankings %>% 
  ggplot(aes(
    x = winpercent
  )) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
  labs(
    title = 'Candies win percent distribution',
    x = 'Win percent',
    y = 'Count'
  )

```


# Data viz - more than one variable

## Exercise 4

How about using the both variables; chocolate vs winpercent? Run the following incomplete code snippet to get a faceted visualization.

Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent, fill = caramel)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~chocolate)

```


- Consider adding the `fill = caramel` within the aes() vs. geom_histogram(), what do you get?
- _The graph of winpercent based on whether it contains caramel and chocolate._

## Exercise 5

Create a visualization that examines the relationship between a candy’s win percentage and whether it contains chocolate. Include x and y labels and a title. Describe any relationship you see.

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = winpercent
  )) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~chocolate) +
  labs(
    title = 'Candies win percentage based on it chocolate content',
    x = 'Win percentage',
    y = 'Number of candies'
  )

candy_rankings %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = winpercent
  )) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~caramel) +
  labs(
    title = 'Candies win percentage based on it caramel content',
    x = 'Win percentage',
    y = 'Number of candies'
  )

candy_rankings %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = winpercent
  )) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~fruity) +
  labs(
    title = 'Candies win percentage based on it fruit content',
    x = 'Win percentage',
    y = 'Number of candies'
  )
```
- _Candies which contain chocolate generally have higher win percentage. Mean and median confirm it._
- _There is not a lot of data for candies containing caramel, but it appears that whether a candy contains it or not has no effect on its win percentage. Based on the mean and median, candies containing caramel have higher win percentage._
- _Fruity candies have smaller win percentage. Mean and median confirm it._ 


- Consider the similar pair by replacing chocolate with caramel, fruity and compare their results. 
- Also include summary statistics details for this discussion by using the calculation below: 

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  group_by(fruity) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_win = mean(winpercent),
    median_win = median(winpercent)
  )
```


## Exercise 6

Do more expensive candies win more often? Make a scatterplot of pricepercent (x) against winpercent (y). Describe their relationship.  

```{r}
candy_rankings %>% 
  ggplot(aes(
    x = pricepercent,
    y = winpercent,
    colour = chocolate,
    shape = bar
  )) +
  geom_point()

```
_There doesn't seem to be much correlation._

- Add `color = chocolate` to add a third variable to the created visualization
- _For candies containing the chocolate, the higher the price higher win percentage. For candies without chocolate, the trend is opposite._
- How to facet this by using another categorical variable such as `bar`? 
- _By adding shape or size or level of transparency._

## Exercise 7

Are chocolate candies more likely to be candy bars? Make a filled bar plot with chocolate on the x-axis and fill = bar. Describe what you see.

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = chocolate,
    fill = bar
  )) +
  geom_bar()

```
_Yes, chocolate candies are more likely to be bar candies than not-chocolate candies._

## Exercise 8
Create a new variable called price per sugar ratio as the division of pricepercent and sugarpercent. Plot it against winpercent, and set the color of all points to blue for the competitors who are not "One dime" or "One quarter". Include x and y labels and a title. Describe any relationship you see.

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  mutate(
    price_per_sugar = pricepercent / sugarpercent,
    type = case_when(
      competitorname == 'One dime' | competitorname == 'One quarter' ~ 'special',
      TRUE ~ 'normal'
    )
  ) %>% 
  #filter(type == 'normal') %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = price_per_sugar,
    y = sugarpercent,
    colour = type
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "normal" = "blue",
      "special" = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = 'Price per sugar ratio vs Sugar percentage',
    x = 'Price per sugar ratio',
    y = 'Sugar percentage',
    colour = ''
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```
- _The 'One dime' and 'One quarter' seem to be extreme values and significantly deviate from the norm. If we remove them from the visualization, we can see the data more clearly. The higher the sugar percentage, smaller the price per sugar ratio._

## Exercise 9

Modify your plot in Exercise 8 to facet by whether a candy is bar-shaped. Have the color reflect whether the candy is fruity or not. The plot must include x and y labels along with a title. How do these plots compare to each other?

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  mutate(
    price_per_sugar = pricepercent / sugarpercent,
    type = case_when(
      competitorname == 'One dime' | competitorname == 'One quarter' ~ 'special',
      TRUE ~ 'normal'
    )
  ) %>% 
  filter(type == 'normal') %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = price_per_sugar,
    y = sugarpercent,
    colour = fruity
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      'FALSE' = "blue",
      'TRUE' = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = 'Price per sugar ratio vs Sugar percentage',
    subtitle = 'By fruit content and candy type',
    x = 'Price per sugar ratio',
    y = 'Sugar percentage',
    colour = ''
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~bar)

```
